Where Deals Are Lost

Where an Insurance Site Loses the Buyer Before the Call

The ProblemStandard Agency

Legal strikes the product page after launch

A policy page written to sell reads as a promise to pay. Compliance rewrites it after launch, the campaign window closes during the second pass, and the page that goes back up explains nothing a broker can act on.

The carrier's reviewer cannot find the security page

Before a carrier or reinsurer takes the call, someone on its risk team opens the site to check licensing, data handling and certifications. A badge in the footer with nothing behind it sends that person back with the box unticked.

One disclosure changes and forty pages fall behind

Per-state and per-market wording lives in footnotes copied by hand across the site. When a regulator changes one line, the pages nobody remembered keep the old version, and the marketing lead hears about it from legal.

The SolutionThe Legency Approach

Product pages explain cover without promising it

Triggers, exclusions and claims handling are written in language compliance has already approved, so the page clears review on the first pass and the launch keeps its date.

Trust detail sits where a risk team looks

Licensing, SOC 2, ISO 27001, data residency and subprocessors on one page that exists before anyone asks. The reviewer finds what they were sent for, and the site says the contract is safe to sign.

Disclosures update once and change everywhere

Per-market wording lives in a shared component. Your team edits it in one place, every page carrying it updates, and the change record shows who changed what and when.

Compliance on the Page

Carriers Read the Site Looking for a Reason to Stop

Insurance website design starts with the reviewer. A carrier, reinsurer or enterprise risk team will open the site before the first meeting, and what they cannot find they assume is missing.

Licensing detail that reads as evidence

Which markets you are licensed in, under which entity, with the regulator named. A footnote written that way answers the reviewer's first question. A footnote that only says "regulated" invites a second one.

Policy wording that survives review

A product page has to explain a policy without promising a payout. Written for the review it will face, it clears legal on the first pass. Written to sell, it gets rewritten after launch and ends up saying nothing a broker can use.

A security page for the reviewer sent to check

SOC 2, ISO 27001, data residency and subprocessors on one page linked from every product page. K2 Group put us through a 36-question cyber due-diligence questionnaire and a client-side MSA before work started, and that questionnaire is the model for what a carrier's reviewer will ask of you.

A change record for the regulator's question

Knowing which wording was live on which date matters more in insurance than in most sectors. A build with a change record answers the question a regulator or an auditor will eventually ask, and answers it without a search through old emails.

Long Sales Cycles

Brokers Ask an Assistant Before They Ask a Provider

A considered purchase, a cycle measured in quarters, and a buyer who starts by asking which providers even cover the peril. That is the shape of question an AI assistant now answers with a shortlist.

The shortlist forms before the first call

When a broker asks which parametric or embedded providers cover a risk and the assistant names three, a provider it leaves out is off the list before anyone at that company knows the question was asked.

Being wrong is worse than being absent

Assistants describe companies from stale sources, so an insurer can be named for a line it withdrew or a market it left. Measuring what is said each month is the only way to find that before a broker does.

The measurement already runs for clients

ChannelSight, a client in another sector, is the most-cited domain in its AI answer set at 16 of 56 answers. Blueflame AI's citations are tracked monthly against its named competitors. The same panel runs for an insurer against the providers its brokers compare.

Case Study

Sold through enterprise procurement to regulated buyers.

Blueflame AI sells agentic AI to investment firms whose risk teams read a vendor's site before the first call. The engagement has run 18+ months through enterprise procurement, a funding round and an acquisition by Datasite, with a monthly evidence report in one unchanging format throughout.
